This is just a general function to update the HDR properties of the rendering context. You mentioned (in relation to `surface_set_hdr_output_reference_luminance`):

> Whenever window_set_hdr_output_max_luminance(...)

So this is just called to update that property.

> When maximumExtendedDynamicRangeColorComponentValue or 

This property changes dynamically in response to screen brightness and ambient light, which I verified by shining my iPhone light towards the screen.

> maximumPotentialExtendedDynamicRangeColorComponentValue of the surface change. This may happen as the window is moved to different screens, for example.

Correct, however it is actually because the screen property of the NSWindow has changed.

Per the [Apple documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsscreen/maximumpotentialextendeddynamicrangecolorcomponentvalue?language=objc), this value never changes for a given screen:

> The value of this property is determined when you create the NSScreen object, and doesn’t change afterwards.

Conclusion is that we only update the reference luminance when the window changes screen.
It is updated each time the window changes screens, as this value is **fixed** according to Apple's documentation

The idea behind `linear_luminance_scale` was to configure how the range 0 to 1 was expressed in the linear color space, mostly due to the lack of specification for what that should be.

Since Apple's platforms all seem to agree that the range 0 to 1 should map to the SDR range (where 1 = reference luminance), it seems fine to return reference luminance as the scaling factor and leave this doing nothing.

If that changes however and one of the platforms is different, then this may need to be implemented.

**EDIT:** This comment was incorrect and the hardware reference luminance is actually 100.0 on iOS. See https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123082 for details.

In one of the ACES developer meetings, I remember hearing one of the developers say in exasperation under their breath that the iOS reference luminance is 203 nits instead of 100 nits. Indeed, this appears to be the case: changing these constants to 203 nits makes Godot's iOS HDR report luminance values that appear to be in the right ballpark. It's possible that 203 nits is not exactly correct, but it's definitely a lot closer than 100 nits for iOS. The two common reference luminances used for HDR video content are 100 nits (cinema) and 203 nits (HDR alongside SDR content).

Because this is a constant magic number, I suggest adding a new constant to this file:

```
static constexpr float HARDWARE_REFERENCE_LUMINANCE = 203.0f;
```

This "hardware reference luminance" is the threshold where the entire display will have its gain dropped. Going below 203 nits just dims the entire screen in hardware with the software (Godot) being entirely unaware of this happening. Going above 203 nits is where the hardware behaviour remains constant and the brightness adjustment happens purely in software, giving us the EDR behaviour that we expect. 

```suggestion
	float max_luminance = _screen_potential_edr_headroom() * HARDWARE_REFERENCE_LUMINANCE;
```

**NOTE:** I have no idea how things work on visionOS and have no way of testing. In the end, it doesn't matter too much because neither the game developer or player will be able to adjust max or reference luminance values through Godot. Worst case is the luminance values are not physically accurate on visionOS like they are on macOS and iOS.
